newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire force leader sees refugees, talks with rebels.
newsitem.headline: Zaire force leader sees refugees, talks with rebels.

text.p: Lieutenant-General Maurice Baril, Canadian commander of the proposed intervention force for eastern Zaire, said he passed up to 40,000 refugees on Thursday on his intial trip into the area.

Baril visited the rebel-held city of Goma to discuss the proposed force with Zairean rebel chief Laurent Kabila, who shares the Rwandan government's view that there is no need for military intervention.
"We discussed the question of deployment of military intervention and anything I do I will coordinate with him," he said, without elaborating.
Baril, who declined to speak further, headed to the eastern Zairean town of Minova outside Goma, finding large numbers of refugees along the road.
"We went to Minova where there were lots of refugees, perhaps 40,000 on the road, and I think they will come to Sake (near Goma) at midday tomorrow." he said.
"Lots of folks are worried about their condition as they can't break away from the group and come on down," the Canadian general said.

Journalists who tried to follow his convoy west of Goma were blocked at Sake, and fled when shots were fired from hills above the town. The shots, which did not injure anyone, did not appear to have been aimed at Baril.
Amid dwindling international concern, Baril is trying to put urgency into efforts to bring food to Rwandan Hutu refugees still in eastern Zaire.

There were an estimated 1.2 million refugees before fighting between the rebels, Zairean troops and Hutu extremists forced them from their camps. In mid-November up to 600,000 went home to Tutsi-dominated Rwanda, which they had fled in 1994 fearing reprisals for the genocide of up to a million Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
The Canadian government, still anxious to act, has proposed air-drops of food into eastern Zaire despite the opposition of the Zairean government.
"The Zairean government is categorically opposed to the Canadian proposition to drop foodstuffs for refugees and displaced Zaireans," Information Minister Boguo Makeli said.

He said Zaire had doubts about the safety of dropping supplies and objected to missions originating in neighbouring countries it accuses of aggression. Aid workers dismissed the idea as dangerous and expensive.

One Nairobi-based aid worker said the idea showed "impotence and desperation" among countries: "How do you airdrop supplies when you have no clue as to the whereabouts of the people you are supposed to be helping?"
Refugees who have gone home were mostly from camps around Goma, at the northern tip of Lake Kivu, which forms part of the border between Zaire and Rwanda.
Refugees from near Bukavu on the southern shore of Lake Kivu have been harder to trace. Aid workers said more were coming out of the forest on Thursday, clearly suffering from hunger.

At least 1,500 refugees emerged from forests on Thursday, heading for Bukavu. Refugees crossing at Bukavu said they believed at least 100,000 refugees was being driven by Hutu militiamen towards Walikale, about 50 km (30 miles) west of the Bukavu-Goma road.
